I know this is a early access game and that it comes with all the downsides of not being a complete game, but I agreed that it was worth buying it to at least try the game. I didn't play the demo (maybe a mistake, maybe not), but that's how things are. The concept, images and videos available here attracted me, I mean, a stock market sim (which i have never seen, btw f the market), with some 80's to 90's anime look, with an interface like it was made in the 80's? That's new to me. 

Anyway, I bought the game and waited for it to download... played a little bit of other games while at it and noticed, it had already downloaded, as it was less than 100 mb (I'm being serious, you could probably run this game in a potato with screen). Booted up the pc (because the game runs on a pc screen, got it?) and got hit with an OS screen just like the 80's. Cool, this game stays true to it's aesthetic. 

Started the game on CEO Mode (there's also free mode which I haven't tested and story mode which isn't available right now, as it's in early access), and Amy talked to me, she's gonna be your personal advisor through the whole game. Started getting into the screens and trying to understand what each thing mean, as it's a little bit overwhelming at first with many options and numbers, as the market it, but maybe a much more dumbed down version. While still trying to understand, the Yakuza talked to me (an event that only happens when you have a company i guess? And I might point out that it looks different from the rest of the game, as they used a pixelated real photograph, probably the only in the game), another dude stepped up as the CEO of KOMAMI (yes, they use real companies with edited names, and the art of his face gives me some kind of 80's duck hunt aesthetic, differently from Amy, that's a much more complex art with shadows and highlights... maybe the more complex are the ones that you meet in person?), I got hit with a call with insider information (Cool! Let's get rich!) and then a random calling me to hang out. We went to the arcade, and well... it was great, there's loads of mini games and things to try, which got me quite impressed, as there's much more thing to do in this game than just trying to make money in the stock market, and as a plus you build the relation with those weird pixelated faces.

After a while, I built a nice portfolio, while being called to answer the financial services agency, as I made some unusual trading activity and got hit with a setback, some millions out of my account as I f'd up. Also, while doing a whole lot of trading, my company (which you create when you start the campaign) went under. I dare to say it's pretty hard to stay afloat in the first gameplay, as you have not much money to invest in it. I had to resign and kept building my portfolio. Some time later, I found out that I could invest in the real state market, and while not being the most profitable decision, it was pretty safe. 

I played this game for a while, around 4,5 hours in a wednesday starting at 2 am, so yea, I saw the sunrise at the corner of my eye while operating in the market and building my second company. There I saw loads of things that I won't spoil the surprise, but all in all, this game was pretty entertaining. It surprised me a lot when I started and even more while I got paced through the 4,5 hours. The aesthetic is amazing, staying true to it's 80's set up most of the time (there was some decisions that I just accepted as the games looks even better), the art is 10/10. The environment of the game with all the possibilities as to what to do, where to explore, how to build your portfolio, was pretty good. All in all, the simulator part of the game is great. 

With all this things written, I do recommend this game, it's still in early access but it's worth a couple hours of play time. There was a couple of things that I questioned, as to where wasn't any other company joining as two of them went under, but after some time, SUBERU, joined the market doing an IPO. So yeah, other companies do appear, but it's still kinda limited the number of companies available in the market at the same time. You can also start noticing some events repeating themselves over and over again after you play for some time, so that might be something to improve (but it's not bad as it's currently is, it only has a margin to improve), maybe variety, random events, maybe even turning the dial up in the life sim events? Who knows? More random and funny events might be something cool to add. Or maybe more serious ones? Who knows? There was one thing I didn't understand, the historic setup, is it really true? Where's the events regarding what happened there? Are those stocks rising and plummeting true to the time? Did Nissan or Lissan plummeted in 82? What does the historic option means?

Again, I do recommend this game, as it's cheap and it's good. It's a visual novel with a dumbed down version of the market, and the lesson here is, the more money you have, the more room you'll have to play with, buying insider information or taking advantage of the market as you shall experience if you play the game. In stocks (and life!), there's the rich one and we, middle class and poorer that think they can make a quick buck in stocks, well... you'll probably lose most of the time. But in the game it's decent. Maybe a realistic difficulty? I don't know, it might be nice to see the market crashing and everything going to s**t, literally. 

Anyway, waiting for the story mode!

Stonks 9800 is a rare gem in the stock‑trading game genre because it doesn’t take itself too seriously. Unlike other titles that treat investing as a dry simulation, this game embraces the fact that it’s a game and leans into the fun. The quirky minigames make you feel like a true investor or stockbroker navigating the hustle of 1980s Japan, and they add a playful layer that keeps the experience fresh and engaging.  

The retro computer interface is another highlight—it perfectly captures the vibe of the era and adds a surprising amount of immersion. Every detail feels intentional, and it’s clear the developer poured genuine care and passion into crafting this world. Stonks 9800 isn’t just about trading stocks; it’s about living the fantasy of being part of that unique time and place, and it nails that feeling brilliantly.

Like any good stock broker, I knew that if I wanted to make waves in the market, I had to dive in. There wasn't time to dip in my toes, test the temperature. You won't get anywhere in life if you never take risks.

So I sold my house.

And with that nest egg slowly bleeding out of my hands due to rental housing, I got to work. I watched the market, I bought low, I sold high. There's no such thing as diamond hands for bottom feeders like us. Diamond hands are for the rich. And we're not rich. Even if it was a 10 yen profit, I took it. It all adds up, and slowly, gradually, I was trading in ten stocks instead of three. I was making hundreds of thousands of yen instead of tens.

It was slow going. For a while, it seemed that I had the opposite of Midas' Touch, every stock I bought turned to ashes in my hands almost immediately. Even at a company's lowest point, it sunk even further with my foul shares being bought. Then, one weekend while relaxing at the bar with my peers, I overheard them talking about the market. Pretending these nameless, faceless drunkards were my friends, I butted in. Insider knowledge. A company with dirt cheap stocks is about to have a massive upswing. This was it. My big break.

I sold everything. I took a loan. All of my assets, everything I can muster. All in.

It was a perilous, nail-biting week. Were they full of it? Was I doomed.

No. Because like I said: You never get anywhere if you don't take risks.

I saw that blue line shoot a 90 degree angle straight up to the sky. It made the other stocks look insignificant in comparison. I dumped it, all of it. And then? I shorted them. Took as many stocks as they'd give me. Within two weeks, I had taken them to the cleaners, and I came out of it a multimillionaire. I bought my house back, I bought myself a car, and I could finally be declared a somebody in this field. People reached out to me for investments, loans, promising it'll come back in turn. And it certainly came back.

As the years went by, my bank account was no longer a number, it was a rolling tide. It rose and fall, but it always came to a steady medium, one that was always getting higher. I didn't see the amount of stocks I was buying, I saw the percentage of the company I was buying. It wasn't about the money anymore. It was about the status.

I don't want to be a stockbroker.

I want to be a kingpin.

The millions turned to billions. The different colored lines were just that, lines. I had such a significant stake in the market that I practically owned it. I can make or break these companies in a single day. When they go down, I inject enough money for them to recoup their losses tenfold. Then when they rise, I short them, and I sell everything. Sure, it was illegal. But who cares? 

They can't touch me. I'm a billionaire.

I had the best lawyers in Japan.

My villa was akin to that of Scarface's mansion, I had a veritable fleet of limos and sports cars, kept in peak condition, one for each day of each month of each year. I had it all. The money, the women, the power.

Not even the yakuza can touch me.

But even I know it won't last. They'll build their case against me some day. No sins go unpunished for too long. But they'll never forget me. And I hope you won't either.

Take my story as an inspirational tale. When you start out, trading penny stocks and living out of your car, remember that I was there too. And I made it. And so can you.

I have fallen in love with this game and am so excited to see how it it evolves.

Most of the reviews bring up how fun the trading mechanic is (and the assistant Amy) but what I really LOVE about this game are the aesthetics and theming. The CRT monitor effects meant to mimic an old 80s desktop computer, along with the phenomenally addictive music (I love the main menu theme so much that I always listen to it for several minutes before I start) make this into a truly unique and artistic experience that sets it apart. It's the specificity of the setting that I love the most. There are many, many other games that feature trading mechanics, including stock trading. However, there are no other games that I can think of that simulate being a Japanese stock trader in the 1980s. Yakuza 0 definitley nails the 80s Japan aesthetic but as the gameplay is mostly about fighting it doesn't focus on the business side very deeply. STONKS 9800 scratches that itch for me.

If there are any suggestions I could make for the developer I would personally love to see more roleplaying mechanics. I want to be able to create my own character, complete with their own name and picture. Being able to buy more luxury goods and other things to spend money on, and just generally more to do outside of just trading. The future updates look like they will address this and the developer seems dedicated to this project so I'm quite excited to see how this title evolves. As it is though its a very fun title that has a way of just keeping you addicted and wanting to keep playing. 

If you love the basic Buy Low, Sell High mechanics of trading games, have any sort of interest in the stock market, and are a fan of 1980s computer aesthetics, this is the game for you. Playing this makes me feel like a coked out stockbroker in 1984, excitedly watching a line go up a chart while snorting lines off of my desk. Great work Ternox!

Just a review for the Steam Awards, I've nominated Stonks 9800 for the visual category because it genuinely does have a fantastic identity and knows exactly what it is aiming for and how to create it. Lovely game. Even the Yakuza. Nice boys...

[h1]Hey there![/h1]

Personal thoughts and knowledge:
I've been training under a junior hedge fund manager as an analyst for the last three years, and I would have to say that this game encompass some of the more fun aspects of the stock market. Such as managing relations, and legal guidance according to the law and enforcement such as SEC etc (insider trading junk). My understanding is that the financial reports you can pull from Amy are equivalent to those of financial reports like 10K documents(annual reports to shareholders). Personally, I like to play the game without the phone calls from friends that mention insider knowledge of the companies and purely trade off the abilities of the board members and C level management in combination with the awareness of how the industries are performing.

[b]Positive Comments:[/b]

Numbers going up gives me happiness. But seriously, I really like the fact that companies can be in dry spells for your entire play-through of the game. It just depends on how your market plays out given the news/who all is employed by the company and their abilities. I think for the first 4 years I played the game, I had a company "Capcon" that performed like sh*t for the entire period I played. However, a different series played out for company "NT" where new management took over, and the value continued to hold its own in comparison to the other organizations. It's nice to know that the features included in the game actually play into each other and aren't just there for non-sensible pop-ups.

I also like that the weekends act as the "after hours" where companies typically exchange shares or contracts conclude.

[b]Constructive Criticism:[/b]

I believe there are some quality of life changes that could be made but maybe this is me just wanting to inherently optimize my workflow within the game. Typically I'll have my own layout (irl) where I can organize information or write down recent information and how that correlates to similar past events that I've kept track of. I feel like this could be a really fascinating mechanic that could be included adding an extra depth of difficulty and an ability to track and retain information from the market. It would just be up to the player to track it properly or be potentially punished for tracking improper information. This would also allow the Developers to continually add new events that cause mayhem without throwing the players into the dirt before they understand what the event will potentially result in.

I also feel like there could be more categorization. What I mean by this; stock earnings reports, annual reports and lists of information in general (just some examples) could allow for filters that allow you to measure the companies from top to bottom in order of highest valuation or dividend yield (vise-versa as well). This feature could be available for purchase for the player in "November 19, 1987" as this is when "Microsoft Excel" debut and was revolutionary in the financial industry when organizing and orchestrating information. This would force the player to get used to the order of things for the first three years and then allow them to organize information more complexly.

I am very excited for the story mode, and more complex events that take place and a greater difficulty!

[b]Final Thoughts:[/b]

You really can't go wrong with this game if you're really checking it out in the first place. Definitely for a niche community here on steam but nonetheless a fun experience. I think it would be pretty funny if this game ended up so close to the real deal that it was used for training. I think of like racing sims when that comes to mind, and how professionals run courses virtually to prepare themselves for the various environments that occur in their professional runs.

[h1]What is STONKS?[/h1]

    STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator is exactly what it says there on the cover. It is of course, a game, so expect some whacky stuff you wouldn't expect in real life (though not too whacky).

    In this game, you create your own character and play as them. There are not a lot of customization options, at least in appearance, but you do get to choose among perks that may help or hinder you (or both) for your playthrough.

    You spend most of your time looking through different management screens / interfaces. These screens are mostly graphs for the market price of different stocks and commodities as well as sheets detailing different companies. You also get interfaces for your character's status and profile as you do have to manage your character's well-being as part of the gameplay. As you play, there will be prompts that explain various news about the conditions of the different companies, as well as your character's well-being.

    Perhaps I'm making it sound a little too boring, but note that there are also multiple mini-games to be found. There's a fishing mini-game, a claw-hand mini-game, a pachinko mini-game, a poker mini-game, a golf mini-game, and so on. But mostly, yes, most of the gameplay is about watching lines go up and down and then rushing to go buy or sell stocks. There is a prevalent theme of chances / gambling as this permeates through the selection of mini-games (notice how they are all chance-based with the exception of the golf mini-game).

    Finally, there is Amy, the mascot you see on the front, and there seems to be an under-implemented dating-sim mini-game (?). Of course, the game isn't finished developing, but there seems to be a groundwork for that. The game makes no shortage of notices for when you improve your relationship with her, your advisor.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Evaluation[/h1]

Disclaimer: I do not have any experience trading, nor have I ever worked as part of a financial institution, so I cannot give a definitive evaluation of the accuracy of this game regarding the stock market's volatility.

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
(7/10)

    As I have expressed in the first sentence of this review, I adore the graphics of this game. Maybe it's just nostalgia, but I love how the graphics are curved as if I was viewing this in an old-school CRT monitor. I also love the developer's choice to make the graphics pixelized. Something about these design choices make me feel like an old-school professional in the late 80's / early 90's. 

    On a less enthusiastic note, the character profile picture and the NPC's profile pictures are all using reusable parts (I mentioned earlier that the game has character customization). Unfortunately, I find this part of the game less appealing. I wish this part would get remade. This is in sharp contrast with Amy, who has detailed art down to the midsection, [strike]just above the knees[/strike]. I understand this game is in development, but seeing Amy this detailed makes me wish there were more people with more "character" in the game. Some minigames also leave something to be desired, particularly the fishing mini-game and the horse-betting mini-game. I understand that these were meant to give off a retro video-game feel, but I feel as if these can still be improved without stepping over that.

[h2]Music[/h2]
(6/10)

    The music is great as well. The game goes through seasons. Every time I am just about to be sick of the current background music, the season changes, and the music changes along with the interface. The music is kept fresh and I appreciate that.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
(6/10)

[h3]No Handholding[/h3]
    As someone who did not have prior experience to trading, I found the gameplay interesting. At the start of a new game, you create a character with some short-descript perks, and then you are dropped into the management screens with no instructions on how to proceed. That's how I like it. I like a game that doesn't hold my hand, but has that option when I need it. It is a game where you explore what you can do. That last screen in the game is the "Advisor" screen which is where you can talk to Amy and there is an option to get hints. She doesn't really say anything about click here or click there, but rather, because this is a simulator, she tells you the general idea of how real-world ideas are projected in the game. For example, she tells you how to get "reputation" and what you can do with "reputation".

[h3]Skill Issue..?[/h3]
    With that said, majority of the game is looking at lines go up-and-down. And sometimes, you just let it do that for a solid few minutes. This is for when you want to earn money with dividends (money earned passively per month from the companies you have invested in). Fair enough, since this is a simulator, it may just be a skill issue if your gameplay is mostly that. The game doesn't encourage nor discourage you from just endlessly waiting on your dividends. Of course, there is always a possibility that the company that has your investments goes bankrupt, but like I said, this is a game where you explore what you can do. It's up to you if you want to make bold moves or safe moves. I like that about it. I said before that I am interested as someone who has never touched the stock market and that is because I can safely touch that experience with a simulator such as this.

[h3]Mini-games[/h3]
    To break up that experience however, there are mini-games. I find that these games do a good job at being palette-cleansers especially since they are varied. Some of these mini-games are unlocked as you go through the game, so the game doesn't throw this all in your face at once. Some of these games can actually have an impact in the main gameplay, particularly pachinko and poker. In these games, you can earn large sums of money or in the case of poker, assets such as real estate. And of course you can take huge losses in these as well. Other games have collectibles and the game graciously helps you keep track of them. Unfortunately, most of these games are still just the same gambling or chance-based calculation gameplay as the main game. After a while, they too can get tiresome. It would be nice if there were other types of games, though as it is, it's fine. Personally, it gives me a natural point for taking a break from the game.

[h3]Other[/h3]
    As I have mentioned, there seems to be an underdeveloped part of the game with Amy. I am honestly interested in that and wish to see more in the future.

    Another thing I would like to see improved is the interactions with the NPCs. As it stands, I barely go into the contacts screen to bother talking with the NPCs. I also don't see the point of bothering to improve my relationship with these people. For now, that contact list just keeps getting bigger and harder to keep track of without any reward for it. I suppose I'm just supposed to feel good about being popular? I might just be missing some hidden gameplay since I'm only 9 hours in, at the time of writing.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Summary[/h1]
(6.3/10)

    STONKS has very good potential. As it currently is, it is already fun for me, someone who has never entered the stock market scene before. The interface is nice and nostalgic, as well as the music. If you enjoy looking at multiple different screens to optimize resources, this is the game for you. However, if you're looking for blood-pumping action, interactive NPCs, or realistic graphics, better look elsewhere.

Similarly to The Invisible Hand, Stonks is an arcade take on stocks that allows you to long and short stocks to make money, spend it on property and cars. However it is imo better executed in ways than Invisible Hand. The game happens strictly within the oldschool computer monitor and there is no interruption inbetween days and weeks. Time scale flows much quicker in the game but the indexes only tick each day. Depending on how much pausing or forwarding you do a year of gameplay time can be up to an hour real time that goes by real quick as you find yourself chasing numbers hard.
Stonks becomes more interesting over time as you can start a company, or become CEO or a board member of an existing company if you manage to hold a large enough share of stocks in it. As well as dividends being a factor, holding stock in certain companies award healthy monthly pay. Buying a better house, and a car will increase your comfort allowing you to maintain better health at work. Property you don't live in awards rent. 
Random events influence markets and social events also happen that do not require much involvement from you most of the time if are not interested. However bar crawls and pachinko sessions will increase your relationship with the characters you come across. Each of these characters operating positions at the various companies in the game world.
Company management which for now is fairly basic but is a cool feature that allows you finally do something about the relationships you built with random NPCs over time. Company management is more or less about balancing budget, expanding departments and placing skilled friends and hires in managerial positions to get better results from your marketing campaigns, product launches and developments, driving your stock and your company forwards. 
As time goes and your wealth increases the general average values of the initial and additional stocks goes up meaning while you can be extremely wealthy you are still far from being able to easily take everything over and finish the game. There is still plenty to add to the game to expand on all of these mechanics but in it's current early state it is already a lot of fun.

I traded stocks until I raised enough capital to start a company of my own. I built it from the ground up, and it became successful beyond my wildest dreams. Before I knew it, I was controlling the company with the largest market cap on the stock exchange, and rapidly moving up the list of the most influential people in Tokyo. I was living a life of incredible comfort with my expensive car and large single family home. No more public transportation and shared walls for me.

Then it happened. A failed product launch, followed by a market crash. My arrogance had gotten the best of me; we incurred deep losses and I had failed to keep enough in our reserves for us to stay afloat. I watched as the morale of all of my faithful employees plummeted. People who I'd spent so much time cultivating relationships with. All the nights we spent drinking together and sharing stock tips. All the days we spent talking about our lives over personal phone calls. All down the drain. They left, one by one, often insulting me or the company on their way out.

I tried to stop the bleeding every way I could. I tried to keep entire departments from collapsing. But it was hopeless. So I did the only thing I could think of: I resigned. Investors were thrilled that I was leaving, and our stock went [i]up[/i]. The company went on to recover without me. But I had already sold all of my shares, as I thought they were going to become worthless. I should have waited to sell. One final mistake by a failure of a CEO.

I tried to fill the void with high risk activities like pachinko, betting on horses, and underground poker tournaments. But it didn't work. Of course it didn't work.

Amazingly, Amy stuck by me through everything. She's a saint, and I don't deserve her. But I'm so lucky to have her, because her relentless optimism opened my eyes to one very important thing:

It's only 1990, and I've still got one billion yen.

It's not over yet. Not by a long shot.

Have you ever put the $10000 grandma gifted you before her untimely death in the stock market? Right into some shady tech company that failed two months afterwards, causing you to cry yourself to sleep as your initial capital has plummeted to a measly 50 cents? That wouldn't have happened in 1980's Japan, and it wouldn't have happened in STONKS-9800.

This game is essentially a power fantasy for the amateur stock market investor. Buy low, sell high, get money. Take that money, buy even lower, sell even higher, get more money. Buy a ridiculous amount of stocks, causing the price to skyrocket, sell it the same day, get busted by the financial authorities (nothing your lawyers can't take care of for a fraction of your profits) Get smart and wait for two weeks until you dump the stocks you artificially pumped up.
Why listen to Jim Cramer on how to waste your investments, when you can just go drinking with [CEO OF JAPANESE COMPANY] and have them spill that [JAPANESE COMPANY] will go up 50% next tuesday, allowing you to put all your capital into them on monday? 
What's a 401K? I'm putting 401K BILLION yen into the stocks of [JAPANESE COMPANY] after I, an esteemed professional shareholder, gave an embarassing speech at the latest shareholder meeting, dropping the price from 10000000k yen to 1yen. What a shock, that raises the price of my 1 yen stocks to 10000000k yen again, and just two weeks later I sell at a massive, frankly degenerate profit. Oh my, how fortunate for me, that this financial turmoil happens to just benefit myself!


In all seriousness, this is a fun game for up to 10-20 hours. It emulates early Japanese PC graphics and citypop-type music and does a fairly good job at it. But the real core is the gameplay, the arcadey stock market f*ckery. This is a game where you are mostly looking at charts, purchasing and selling stocks (occasionally real estate and cars, but not really). But unlike real life, those charts feature your company going UP. And it's fun and addictive, your first impulse after making a ludicrously high profit is asking yourself "how do I make EVEN MORE OF A PROFIT?" And then you make that higher profit and wonder how you can MAKE AN EVEN HIGHER PROFIT! You can start your own company and manage that to an extent, get involved with the Yakuza and get into unsavory (yet profitable business) and even just go play pachinko or poker to make your cold hard CASH. 

My only complaint is the lack of replayability and depth. Eventually, you cross off everything that could be done. You created a big company, bought 100 cars, own enough real estate to host a small country, and all you're doing is amassing more and more money on the stock market. (This is accurate to how rich people operate in real life) This stops being fun 10-20 hours into the game, but until then the game is well worth its price, discounted or not.

The game is really good so far. It can take a small bit to get going and to know what you're doing, but once you find a strategy it's super fun. It really gets me thinking and it makes me feel quite immersed honestly. I also really enjoy Amy and think she's an especially nice touch on top of some really good game-play.

This said, there are still a lot of glitches that I hope get patched out in the future. There also a fair amount of tiny things that I hope get improved on in the future.

Examples include: ~When I talk to the Yakuza, the color palette changes from what I set it too. This happens so often it's honestly quite an annoyance, especially since you have to go through every color to change it back to what you like. I wish there was a way to just set the palette and not have it change at all. I understand why it'd change when you talk to them, however with everything else I just stated, if it can't be fixed so it changes back to previous settings, I think it'd be better if the palette just remained the same no matter who you talk to. 

~ There are a fair amount of visual glitches, which don't get in the way of game-play too often but are still quite off-putting, such as during horse races, where if you press the escape key to make it go faster, sometimes the horses will run off screen after crossing the finish line. I also had an instance where Amy tried to talk to me right as I went to the horse race and she was covering the majority of the race screen until it was done.

~ I enjoy the ability to speed up time, however with how slow saving is, in combination with how Amy tends to disrupt game-play when telling you something (i.e: giving you your monthly report.) It unpauses and can often led to disruption. I'll often be trying to buy stocks before the market closes when she pops on screen and then I don't get the chance to continue until the next day. Which isn't too bad, but it is still a mild annoyance.

~ I wish there was a way to buy stocks in bulk, as it can be a bit cumbersome to try and buy stocks in bulk, especially when you have gotten to a point where you are rolling in cash and are just trying to continue that flow. I know it's a very minor thing, but I figured I'd state it since it did bother me a small bit.

~ I also wish that you had more access to the general Yakuza services as it feels like they're out of service more often than not. It feels like you get to use it once a year and then that's it. I understand this is to balance things out, however I think it'd still be nice if you could get to use these services at least two times in one year, as in my opinion I think that'd be fair and not cause too many game-play issues.

Overall this is a really good game and is a load of fun. I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys these kinds of games and wants something to occupy themselves with for a while. I'm excited to see what else the developer does with this title. I'm also really excited for when the story-mode gets released. :)

This game is realistic in that you spend your life almost exclusively on work and the accumulation of wealth, a cog in the machine of capitalism and greed. This game is decidedly [i]unrealistic[/i] in that you have somebody who cares about you. In all seriousness the game’s a bop, especially for being Early Access. Who knew clicking and watching numbers get bigger and smaller could be so much fun. I simply adore the PC-98-inspired look and sounds.

Other than the main gameplay conceit of “Buy! Sell!” there’s multiple mini-games that represent aspects of your work and personal life (golfing to network, unwinding at the arcade, giving a speech to shareholders, etc.) that give some variety. Beyond being a parasitic day-trader you can also build your own company from the ground up, get tangled up with the yakuza, get in trouble with the 80s Japan equivalent of the SEC, and so on.

However I think this would all feel mechanical and empty save for [i]Amy[/i]. Amy gives a vital human reference for everything you’re doing, and makes you feel like you’re struggling to succeed with somebody, and for a purpose, beyond “number goes up”. She is also an opportunity to further expand the game mechanics with light dating sim elements. Not that I’m... lonely or anything, but it actually feels very comforting as she delights in your successes and expresses her concerns without being judgemental.

Game has an ambitious roadmap to further expand what is already easily worth your $10. So if you like the retro anime/VN vibe, stat management, or wholesome dating sims, then STONKS-9800 is worth your money. Just a word of caution the “early game” is a bit slow, but as you get more money and mechanics open up, such fun.

Money is not wealth. It is a system of control, born in debt and shackled to interest. For every U.S. dollar that exists, five more in debt demand repayment — a treadmill that can never be stopped, only sped up. We do not pay off our debts; we pass the burden in circles, a society forever chasing numbers where balance is forbidden by design.

In 1862, Abraham Lincoln issued the greenbacks, interest-free government currency to fund the Civil War without bowing to bankers. In 1865, he was assassinated, and the greenbacks were buried with him. In 1930s Germany, a failed Austrian painter introduced interest-free credit to pull his nation out of collapse. For a brief moment, money served the people instead of the financiers. But this experiment too ended in ruin, crushed by global war and by the powers that profit from debt.

The story repeats across history. In 1881, President Garfield warned that whoever controls money controls the nation — weeks later, he was gunned down. In 1963, John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11110, allowing silver-backed currency to bypass the Federal Reserve. Months later, he was assassinated. In 2011, Muammar Gaddafi pushed for a gold-backed African dinar to free the continent from the dollar system; NATO forces intervened, and he was killed in the desert. Even Andrew Jackson, who fought the Second Bank of the United States in the 1830s and for a moment paid off the national debt, saw his “victory” followed by the Panic of 1837, which threw the nation back into financial bondage.

Every attempt to escape the system ends the same: silenced leaders, ruined nations, or crises that restore the status quo. It is as if debt-money defends itself, striking down anyone who dares to imagine money as a tool of freedom rather than a weapon of control.

Enter "STONKS," the theater of speculation where we pour our wages and hopes into shares of debt-laden companies, mistaking paper promises for wealth. The market rises, it falls — and we celebrate or despair — yet all the while we remain tethered to a system designed to keep us running in place.

The question is not whether you are winning at "STONKS." The question is whether the game itself was ever meant to let you win.

Oh my God this game is something special. This being my first economy game I was a bit unsure as to how exactly I would feel about it, but this game is both so rich with personality, and SO. VERY. ADDICTING. I would often find myself actually having a hard time putting the game down, which was a first for me in a great while.

There's just so much good to say: the game perfectly balances the financial aspect with an equal amount of personality, and it's all topped with an utterly GLORIOUS aesthetic that's very clearly the result of both immense passion and extensive research. Even though I've had minimal experience with a lot of the game's inspirations, I found myself nostalgic for the retro computer style character designs and the absolutely immaculate OST that absolutely nails it in all regards. The game really teleports you into its world, enthralling you with it's depth and charm.

More about that depth, the game itself has SO. MUCH. CONTENT. This especially shines with the fact that this game is still only in early access. It feels like every path you would think you can take, you can. Even a lot of finished games nowadays can't quite nail rewarding the player with this type of freedom, so it's an especial pleasure that this little gem of a game does.

And of course, I couldn't go without showing appreciation to the wonderful, quirky assistant Amy. The game fills her with so much personality, and while it does currently feel like her dialogue is a bit limited, this is something I'm sure will be elaborated upon in future versions. In many ways, her inclusion elevates the overall experience so much. 

Over all, I am very appreciative of this game, and I congratulate the developers on developing such an awesome game. There are so many other little fine details that just make the game feel complete. I am absolutely looking forward to seeing the future additions of mini games, additional gameplay events, and an ENTIRE STORY MODE (ESPECIALLY if it means I get to see more of Amy and her wonderful dialogue). This is a game that, if you like games with a good amount of unique personality, depth, and a quirky side, you should ABSOLUTELY do yourself a favour and purchase. Thank you devs for bringing such a good game out to the world!

As a real-life trader, I was curious how a game could capture the thrill and chaos of the stock market. STONKS-9800 surprised me with it’s simple, retro, and unexpectedly addictive gameplay.

🕹️ Retro Vibes & 80s Japan Setting
Set in 1980s Japan, the game greets you with pixel art and old-school menus. You start by creating a character—not the most advanced customization system, but that’s not the point. Then you choose your difficulty level and how historically accurate you want the market simulation to be. This matters, because every economic event affects stock prices in ways that feel eerily real.

💼 Traits, Capital, and Strategic Depth
Depending on your difficulty, you’ll be given a starting investment fund. Then come the traits—each one gives you unique advantages and disadvantages, shaping your playstyle. From there, you begin your journey as a rookie investor trying to make it big.

🎮 Gameplay That Sucks You In
The retro visuals might turn some people off, but the gameplay? It pulls you in fast. I told myself I’d play for 30 minutes… next thing I knew, hours had passed. Watching a stock you picked skyrocket is pure dopamine. It’s the kind of thrill only traders truly understand.

🏢 From Investor to CEO
The game doesn’t stop at buying and selling. You can become a CEO—either by founding your own company or buying enough shares to take control of an existing one. Every decision you make affects your company’s stock price. And yes, the game even includes short selling, just like in real-world investing.

📈 Realistic, Yet Risk-Free
This game nails the feeling of investing—strategizing, reacting to market shifts, and watching your portfolio grow. But here’s the best part:
Real life investing: spreadsheets, anxiety, and existential dread. STONKS-9800: buy high, sell low, laugh anyway. It’s the only market crash that feels fun.

✅ Final Verdict
STONKS-9800 may look simple, but it’s packed with depth. The retro aesthetic fits the 80s setting perfectly, and the gameplay is so addictive it’ll have you coming back for more. It’s the only place where I can invest recklessly and still sleep peacefully at night.

As someone who works in the finance industry and wanted to make a market sim. himself, I would like to provide some valuable feedback to the devs. which I feel will make the game more interesting:

Having a balance sheet, income statement and cashflow statement for all the companies would be a great addition. Instead of meeting people at the bar and hoping for information on stock price movement, having few financial ratios and fundamental metrics will make for a more interesting play.

While it may seem daunting to the new players to have so much information bombarded at them, the charts would move as a function of both the stock's metrics from the financial statements as well as the insider tips from bars, resulting in a richer gameplay.

Interest on bank loans and charity donation should be tax-deductible because I didn't face any real penalty for being extremely unethical. This would allow players to use debt as capital expenditure to upgrade their own company. A company with bad debt/equity would be more volatile and susceptible to adverse market movements.

Players should be given an option to use leverage, with the tax deductible debt and option to leverage, the players will have more bandwidth to siphon funds from the exchange to their own companies and result in more interesting plays. Each stock could be given a real 'Beta' as a volatility indicator, this makes sure that the market isn't heavily skewed to 1 stock, as this happened with my playthrough with 'Hardbank'.

These are a few additions I believe would make the game more interesting to play, but it is absolutely a solid game and I've had a ton of fun playing this. Really hope the devs. see this, you've been doing an amazing job!

Wow. Okay. Uh. This game. It’s pretty good. Like, alarmingly addictive for what is basically a stock trading sim/tycoon game. It doesn’t seem like it should be as entertaining as I found it to be. It’s not an idler game. You do have to make active investments, check company performance, re-invest dividends, and manage your character’s health and stress. And, it gets even more crazy when you start your own company. You’ll have to manage talent, assign staff in an optimal way, and generally make your company stock inviting to investors. Then you can go out and befriend the board of directors for other competing companies and even poach their staff. 

The game does have some bugs. And, in my opinion, the biggest flaw with the game is the lack of feedback and instruction on some things. Most of this is around the company creation side. For example, if there’s a bottleneck in the company somewhere, there isn’t really any feedback about that except for what Amy (your assistant) tells you. It’s never really explained what’s important to focus on when building out the company. 

I think the game could use a good tutorial and that would solve 80% of the issues. But, even then, if you have a basic understanding of stocks, you can pick up this game fairly easily. Hope this game gets more attention. It’s definitely what I’d consider to be a hidden gem.

STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator, developed and published by TERNOX, is a retro-inspired financial simulation game that transports players to the dazzling, neon-lit world of late 1980s Japan. It’s a game that revels in nostalgia, drawing aesthetic inspiration from PC-98-era interfaces and economic bubble culture while mixing the addictive thrill of stock trading with the humor and eccentricity of indie game design. Beneath its parody title lies a surprisingly engaging experience that blends satire, strategy, and simulation into a compact, entertaining package.

At its core, STONKS-9800 is about making and losing fortunes. Players take on the role of a young investor navigating a simplified version of Japan’s stock market, buying and selling shares across a variety of fictional companies while keeping an eye on personal well-being. The goal isn’t just to amass wealth—it’s also to maintain a balance between profit and sanity. Stress, hunger, and fatigue are just as important as market trends, and neglecting them can derail your success as easily as a bad investment. This fusion of life simulation and trading mechanics gives the game an unusual but entertaining rhythm: one moment you’re analyzing stock graphs, and the next you’re unwinding at the bar, buying sushi, or testing your luck at horse races and pachinko parlors.

The gameplay loop is simple yet engaging. Market data updates dynamically, forcing you to decide when to hold your shares, when to sell, and when to risk everything for a big payout. Real-world logic applies—buy low, sell high—but the game’s humor and unpredictability ensure that luck often feels as important as skill. Your choices affect both your finances and your stress levels, with each in-game day presenting new temptations, random events, and small narrative touches that make the experience feel alive. The charm lies not in realism but in how the game captures the spirit of speculation and greed from Japan’s bubble economy era, all wrapped in a tongue-in-cheek presentation that pokes fun at capitalist excess.

Visually, STONKS-9800 nails its retro aesthetic. The entire interface is designed to look like a late-’80s computer terminal, complete with pixel fonts, chunky icons, and the muted color palette of early financial software. It feels authentic and playful, like a forgotten simulation dug out of an old hard drive. The music amplifies this atmosphere with upbeat city-pop-inspired tracks and jazzy background tunes that perfectly evoke the optimism of the era. The result is an experience that is as much about style as it is about substance. Even when the markets crash and your portfolio burns, it’s hard not to smile at the absurd charm of its presentation.

While the simulation aspect is enjoyable, the game does have its limits. The systems are intentionally lightweight, offering enough complexity to stay engaging without ever becoming overwhelming. Players looking for a deep, realistic economic simulator may find it too shallow; the markets lack real-world intricacy, and some patterns can feel predictable after extended play. The side activities, while fun, can grow repetitive once you’ve seen their outcomes several times. Still, this simplicity is part of the game’s identity—it’s less about mastering algorithms and more about enjoying the ride, embracing both the humor and the chaos of capitalism distilled into pixels.

The game’s accessibility adds to its appeal. It’s easy to pick up, runs smoothly even on low-end hardware, and can be enjoyed in short bursts or longer sessions. The developer’s clear affection for the PC-98 aesthetic and Japanese economic culture shines through in every detail, from the humor-laced item descriptions to the nostalgic sound effects. It’s a love letter to a specific time and place in gaming and economic history, presented through a lens of modern irony. The inclusion of small achievements, collectibles, and visual flourishes gives players reasons to return, even if the core mechanics don’t drastically evolve over time.

STONKS-9800 ultimately succeeds because it understands its audience. It’s not trying to teach financial literacy or simulate Wall Street precision—it’s trying to entertain through absurdity, style, and charm. The mix of stock trading, personal management, and minigames captures the addictive loop of risk and reward, all while laughing at the very idea of getting rich through “stonks.” Its world may be small, its systems simple, but its personality is enormous. For players who appreciate retro aesthetics, tongue-in-cheek humor, and the thrill of chasing profits in a digital bubble, it delivers a surprisingly compelling and memorable experience. It’s a satirical yet affectionate take on greed, luck, and ambition—a reminder that, sometimes, the most rewarding investments are the ones that don’t take themselves too seriously.

[h1]An experience in an experience[/h1]

It is a curious game. Very diverse. There is a LOT to do combined with a retro design for less than 10€. It is a no-brainer just buy this. 

You will start with buying stocks but soon you will discover the joy of pachinko and then the secret poker parties.
Once you buy all the stocks of a few companies you will decide to create yours, financing it by collecting rent and reselling your art collection for a profit. If you are in a bad position your ties with the yakuza will help you out... or not (they seem to have a different definition of what is a good deal in real estate, I bought too many haunted houses because of them). 
With the last update you were introduced to the joy of creating your own charity organization, a way to give back to the community while paying less taxes. But does the community really need all this? You can embezzle money. You will be voted the most influential figure in 1985 Tokyo and will siege in every firm's board deciding of their fate. 
Living a very stressful time you will be a huge donor of next door temple to apaise your mind... or go to the bar to hear the last business rumor. Finally you will spend all your money in the arcade trying to finish your collections or be on the leaderboard.
If you want to take a step back from city life you can take a vacation and go to fish. Which is a fully developed game too.

All in all STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator is a game collection in a game with retro design.

I have a fiendish addiction to games that exist to occupy a fraction of my time. Line go up number fests that make every neuron in my decrepit skull turn on through nothing but sheer benign overstimulation. Cookie Clicker fragmented a part of my psyche back in middle school and I've never been able to outrun the lasting damage it did. So naturally something like STONKS-9800 made sense. The generic business management sim is a market that is either cripplingly unfun Capitalism II style games, or ones that exist to beat you over the head with a brick like Space Warlord Organ Harvesting Simulator. Sitting in the small area of business management and activating my neurons is STONKS. All of the business fun with enough other things packed on to accurately recreate being a business man in 1980's era Japan except I'm not losing as many fingers to the Yamaguchi-gumi.

STONKS places you in Japan, 1980 in a tiny apartment with a bit of money to your name and you must masterfully take advantage of stupid dividend returns, real estate investment and legitimate gambling to become a financial mogul. Your means of getting there manifested through a few token character traits and a slowly expanding roster of stats that allow you to become a master of short selling stocks into the floorboards. Because if you REFUSE to give me my desired buyout, I'm sending your company to Izanami with express delivery. This is already a good framework for a business management game, but STONKS doesn't stop there. Kitschy Famicom graphics and eyesearing color palletes are only the start of various systems that make this an accurate representation of 1980's Japanese life. You must also manage YOURSELF. 

Balancing your four humors of financial well being (phlegm), social well being (red blood), mental well being (black bile) and relations with your secretary (yellow bile) is important to success. Being an insane loner hoarding stocks can get you into the market, but once you have a full company you need to consider more things. You need to take breaks lest you get sent to the hospital, you need to take friends of yours out to drinks and pachinko to get better benefits like insider information and recruitment into the eventual company you'll own. And if you think Amy is just a piece of eye candy to draw in mediocre horny bastards, that's false. That woman is one of the best people you can have for your company if you level relations up enough to get her involved, and she hands you market advice and business deals on a silver platter. She is as important to your financial success as honest means of financial advancement are, such as being a yakuza stoolie and winning apartment leases through smashing the "all in" button. This game is not immune to the Poker Night At The Inventory school of thought. And now I own a house!

The bread and butter that sells STONKS is the meta mechanics, and the various little side games tucked in between the hyperfixation with lines going up. At any point you can elect to just stop doing stock broking and drag an unfortunate friend into a whole host of minigames. Force that mediocre haiku poet to sing 24 Kan Cinderella, make him bet 2 billion yen on a horse named Suzuki Jimny, or go to the pachinko parlor. You will not regret going to the pachinko parlor and somehow turning 50 balls into 1503 because you zoned out and kept mashing the space bar. Engage in the original gacha with the arcade and acqurie 33 stuffed soda cans to mass send to friends and coworkers on Christmas to print good reputation. And don't forget fishing. You'll pop vacation and then spend about 2 hours playing a stupid fishing minigame because you see "REPUTATION WITH AMY +1" and a simian response goes off in your brain. You're not immune to genetic memories of giving Woman a gift, even if that gift is a catfish. 

Engage in unsafe business practices like short selling a stock twice and be detained by the Securities Commission only to be busted out of jail by the Yakuza, bet everything on black and somehow come out on top, purchase every single house, factory and Lawson's in the wider Tokyo area. Nothing is stopping you in this game, not even the Bubble burst. The only thing that keeps you from financial success is realizing you've been playing the same game for 9 hours and you probably should go to bed. And even then, you'll probably hear the music in your sleep. It's infectious.

[h1] Great game with amazing graphics and concerned developers. [/h1]

[h2] Introduction [/h2]
I started playing this game because of Game Grumps. I instantly fell in love with it. The mini games are fun and the different types of investment are very cool. The game is very natural at punishing those who don't diversify and it is great at modeling how volatile the market is.
This is still in early access and there are a lot of quality of life still to be done, but the developers are very concerned about this. We can see through the updates' history that QoL is taken seriously.
The CRT graphics are the best I've ever seen. It truly mimics how it used to be in a way that isn't ugly or tiresome to the eyes.

[h2] About the game [/h2]
[h3] Investments [/h3]
The game offers several ways to invest and make money. You can go to the stock market directly, buy real estate, buy commodities, short sell, create a company and put money on independent projects. All of these are affected by how the economy is going, and there are several factors that you must look into before investing. You can be ethical or not. It is all up to how you want to reach the top.
[h3] Personal life [/h3] 
You have a personal life in this game. There are three main stats: [b] Happiness [/b], [b] Comfort [/b] and [b] Stress [/b]. They are not independent and affect each other. Being too stressed or too unhappy might create bad situations for you. Sickness, not being able to give a speech to shareholders and stuff like that.
In your personal life you also have friends, including your assistant, Amy. You can call them, invite them to go out and send them gifts. These friends can become good sources of information or employees for your company. You can also just have fun with them. There is no need to use people.
[h3] Mini games [/h3]
The mini games are SUPER FUN. They aren't jenky like most mini games, they are usually quick and straight to the point. Some mini games can help you with social relationships like getting gifts from the arcade claw machine.
[h3] Achievements [/h3]
The achievements are good, but need to be tinkered some more. They can get really annoying when they require random stuff like getting a rare toy or fish to appear. The pachinko one, specifically, takes way too long. Aside from minor bugs common to early access games, this is the thing the devs should work more on.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]
If you enjoy tycoon type games, this one is for you. There are many strategies for you to choose and you can carve your path to success the way you enjoy the most. Live your best life in the 1980's Japanese stock market.

Fun little stock trading game where you can also own a corporation and play several mini-games to pass the time between working your self into a stress induced coma.

If virtually getting rich by trading stocks is your kind of jam, this game will definitely scratch that itch... with a catch.

You start by trading small-cap stocks until you accumulate enough wealth. Then, you can buy high-cap stocks or start your own company, which will have its own stock to trade in the market. That's the main hook of the game.

You may wonder, can you do anything with your newfound virtual wealth? Yes! You can buy houses to live in or rent out, and purchase flashy new cars to get to business meetings faster. You can also build relationships with Amy, your secretary/assistant, as well as your business colleagues. There are plenty of activities to engage in, too, presented as minigames, such as playing arcade games, pachinko, golf, and poker, which will help you bond with your colleagues.

Once you build your own company, you can grow it by hiring people and creating departments to increase your company's efficiency and keep your stakeholders happy.

However, while the game excels at simulating stock trading and wealth accumulation, other aspects feel shallow and lack depth. Here are some examples:

- Building relationships, whether with Amy or your colleagues, feels like just filling up a relationship bar. There are no significant perks from developing these relationships. Additionally, the only way to engage in activities with your colleagues is by calling them, but often they're unavailable, making it feel like a waste of time.
- When growing the company, you merely pick from a few options whose outcomes don't feel significantly different. For instance, you can choose to develop new products, but the game doesn't allow you to determine what kind of product to develop.
- You can choose the industry for your company, but they all grow in the exact same way. Running a pharmaceutical company feels the same as running a media and advertising firm.
- Acquiring other companies is too simplistic. I started a very profitable pharmaceutical company and acquired a struggling automotive company, and the only effect was my company's market cap getting bigger. I couldn't choose what to do with the company I acquired.

Given that this is an Early Access game, I hope it will be developed further. The developer is actively adding new features, squashing bugs, and communicating with the community. There's also a story mode version in the pipeline, so I have high hopes that this game will get better over time.

[h2]The anti-monopoly [/h2]

You probably played monopoly at least once in your life. While it is a fun game in the early phase there is a fundamental problem with monopoly: Once one player gets an edge over his competition it's only a matter of time until he bankrupts all of them as there are no comeback mechanics making the game's outcome 100% predictable after a few turns. 

With STONKS-9800 it's exactly the opposite. While in Monopoly everything becomes predictable too soon with STONKS-9800 nothing is predictable at all. Let me guide you through the 1000 flaws in the game you should know about:

- The stocks are not predictable at all. The game tells you there is two ways that influence the stock price: hype and profitability. But hype is actually the only variable you can utilize. You will get random notifications that a stock is going to drastically rise or fall which is your only reliable way to make money in the game. The profitability on the other hand is entirely useless as there is no way to predict future profitability of a business so you can not hope on the long term development of your company. Which leads us to the second major issue:

- You cannot get valid information about how good a company is doing. In theory the game gives you something called "annual reports" which show you whether a company is making money or losing it. But in reality this is not working at all since the reports only show if the company was profitable in the past but not if it is going to be in the future. Addionally the math is not even working. The annual report is not matching the information in the companies profiles for any company. For example the annual report tells you the company was losing 100m last year and the company itself claims it made 10b of profits. It's a total jeopardy to believe either of these numbers. And this problem persists with all companies. On top of that there are bugs with singular companies claiming to have a 300% dividend yield meaning you would actually get 3 times the money you invest back through dividends (which obviously did not happen)

- You can become board member for companies but it's entirely useless. In theory you should be given insider information about the company (which does not happen) and be able to influence decisions in the comapny (which does not happen either)

- You cannot own more than 20% of the shares of each company. After you own that amount there will be not shares left on the market and you will not be able to get any more shares. Technically you can get some through random events but it will only be a insignificant amount (like 0.3% on average) and the events will also be super rare.

- Making friends takes too long. You can make friends in the game only by two ways. Either you get a random friend at each shareholder meeting or you can build a friendship through grinding to call them. You have to call the same NPC about 50 times (every weekend for an entire year) and you will eventually become friends but

- Friends are entirely useless. Most friends offer you nothing at all. You can only hang around with them at a bar to reduce your stress and that's it. And even if you grind some hours to befriend a fellow board member or CEO you still have to invite them to the bar for dozens of times until he eventually agress to sell his 0.3% share in a random company to you. 

- Amy is entirely useless. You can also befriend your assistant in this game. While it will at least not require grinding and happen over time it offers you nothing else than being able to walk with her. While this is fun for once it gets very very boring to listen to the same dialogue again and again. The walk itself is only fluff and does not serve any ingame purposes. 

- The Minigames are my horror. There are two minigames in this game and both of them are just RNG as well. You press a button and hope to randomly win. Not fun at all. And what's even worse there is are three achievement tied to being really really sucessful in pachinko. This alone would lead any sane person to give a thumbs down if it weren't for the more severe problems of this game. 

- The longer you play this game the more the loading times for going to the bar increases. At my savegame if I ever dare to enter the bar it will take 2 minutes until I can leave as the game has problems loading the main menu again. 

I do not even want to start at all the other minor issues like the government randomly changing the income tax every month from 2% to 15% and back to 3% again. The actual economy is neither like monopoly following a strict set of rules nor it is the pure chaos this game is showing you.
